title: Utility Patent
description: The utility patent is the standard patent for new and useful processes, machines, manufactures, compositions of matter, and improvements thereof, under 35 U.S.C. 101. It lasts 20 years from the earliest U.S. filing date and is what most people mean by 'a patent.' Software, mechanical devices, chemical compounds, and business methods (subject to eligibility limits) all file as utility patents.
demo:
from datetime import date
filing = date(2020, 6, 15)
expiry = date(filing.year + 20, filing.month, filing.day)
print('utility patent filed', filing, '-> expires', expiry, '(20 yrs from filing)')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Design Patent
description: The design patent protects the ornamental appearance of an article of manufacture — its shape, surface ornamentation, or configuration — not how it works. Design patents filed on or after May 13, 2015 last 15 years from grant, and the application consists largely of drawing figures showing the claimed design. Icons and graphical user interfaces can be protected as design patents.
demo:
from datetime import date
grant = date(2021, 3, 2)
print('design patent granted', grant, '-> expires', date(grant.year+15, grant.month, grant.day), '(15 yrs from grant, post-2015 filings)')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Plant Patent
description: The plant patent protects a distinct and new variety of plant that has been asexually reproduced — by grafting, budding, cuttings, or tissue culture — other than a tuber-propagated plant or a plant found in an uncultivated state. It lasts 20 years from filing, like a utility patent. Plant patents carry a single claim and detailed botanical descriptions with color photographs.
demo:
print('plant patent: distinct + new variety, asexually reproduced')
print('excludes: tuber-propagated plants, wild uncultivated finds')
print('term: 20 years from filing; one claim')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Provisional Patent Application
description: The provisional application is a low-cost placeholder that secures a filing date for 12 months while the inventor prepares the full nonprovisional application; it is never examined and never becomes a patent on its own. It must still fully describe the invention, because the later nonprovisional can only claim the benefit of what the provisional actually disclosed. Provisionals are the standard 'patent pending' starting point for startups.
demo:
from datetime import date, timedelta
prov = date(2025, 1, 10)
print('provisional filed', prov, '-> nonprovisional due by', prov + timedelta(days=365))
print('never examined; must fully describe the invention')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: PCT International Application
description: The Patent Cooperation Treaty application is a single international filing that reserves the right to seek patent protection in over 150 contracting states. It is not an 'international patent' — there is no such grant; it buys up to 30 or 31 months from the priority date before the applicant must enter the national phase in each desired country. An international search report and written opinion arrive during the PCT phase to guide national prosecution.
demo:
from datetime import date
priority = date(2024, 5, 1)
print('PCT filed; national phase deadline ~30 months from', priority)
print('not a granted patent: one filing, many national entries')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: U.S. National Stage (35 U.S.C. 371)
description: The national stage entry is how a PCT application becomes a U.S. application: the applicant files in the USPTO within 30 months of the priority date, pays U.S. fees, and the application is examined as a regular U.S. nonprovisional. The 20-year term still runs from the international filing date. Missing the 30-month deadline abandons U.S. rights except in narrow revival circumstances.
demo:
from datetime import date
intl_filing = date(2023, 2, 14)
print('371 entry deadline: ~30 months from priority')
print('term runs from international filing date:', intl_filing)
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Continuation Application
description: A continuation is a second application filed while the parent is still pending, claiming the same disclosure and priority date to pursue different claims — typically after the parent's claims are allowed or finally rejected. It lets the inventor keep prosecuting variations without losing the original filing date. Continuations must be filed before the parent issues or goes abandoned.
demo:
print('continuation: same disclosure, new claims, parent still pending')
print('keeps the parent filing date for prior-art purposes')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Divisional Application
description: A divisional application is filed when the examiner issues a restriction requirement, finding the application claims more than one distinct invention; the non-elected inventions are pursued in divisionals that keep the parent's filing date. Divisionals cannot add new matter beyond the parent's disclosure. They are the standard response to restriction, preserving protection for every invented species.
demo:
print('trigger: restriction requirement (multiple distinct inventions)')
print('divisional keeps parent filing date; no new matter allowed')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Continuation-in-Part (CIP)
description: A continuation-in-part adds new matter to a pending parent application while keeping the parent's filing date for the old matter; the new matter gets only the CIP's filing date. CIPs are useful when development continued after the first filing, but the split priority dates complicate prior-art analysis. Many practitioners prefer filing a fresh application for the new matter instead.
demo:
print('CIP: old matter keeps parent date; new matter gets CIP date')
print('split priority -> careful prior-art analysis required')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Reissue Patent
description: A reissue patent corrects an error in an already-granted patent that makes it wholly or partly inoperative or invalid — most commonly claims that were drawn too narrowly. The reissue surrenders the original patent and must be applied for within two years of grant if the correction broadens the claims. Reissue cannot introduce new matter.
demo:
print('reissue: fixes a defective granted patent; original surrendered')
print('broadening reissue must be filed within 2 years of grant')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Reexamination Certificate
description: Reexamination lets anyone (including the patent owner) ask the USPTO to re-examine a granted patent in light of new prior art, resulting in a certificate that confirms, cancels, or amends the claims. Ex parte reexamination is requester-anonymous after filing; inter partes review at the PTAB is the adversarial cousin. It is the main administrative path to challenge or clean up a patent without full litigation.
demo:
print('ex parte reexamination: new prior art -> confirm/cancel/amend claims')
print('certificate attaches to the original patent')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Software-Implemented Utility Patent
description: Software is patented as a utility patent directed to a computer-implemented process, but since Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank (2014) the claims must recite significantly more than an abstract idea — a technical improvement, not merely doing an old process on a computer. Examiners apply the two-step Alice/Mayo framework: first whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, then whether it adds an inventive concept. Drafting focuses on the technical problem solved.
demo:
idea, improvement = 'abstract idea', 'technical improvement'
print('Alice/Mayo step 1: directed to', idea, '?')
print('step 2: claims recite significantly more ->', improvement)
print('draft to the technical problem solved, not the business result')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Business Method Utility Patent
description: Business method patents are utility patents on methods of doing business, examined in USPTO art units that apply heightened eligibility scrutiny after Alice. Historically anchored by State Street Bank (1998) and then narrowed by Bilski (2010) and Alice (2014), they survive only when tied to a concrete technical implementation. Filing strategy emphasizes the system's technical architecture over the commercial method.
demo:
print('State Street (1998) opened the door; Bilski/Alice narrowed it')
print('surviving claims: concrete technical implementation, not the deal itself')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Biotechnology Utility Patent
description: Biotech utility patents cover engineered DNA, proteins, antibodies, cell lines, and therapeutic methods, shaped by Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad (2013), which held naturally occurring DNA segments are not patentable merely because isolated. Claims therefore target synthetic constructs, modified sequences, and methods of use. Written-description and enablement scrutiny is intense: the specification must show possession of the claimed genus.
demo:
print('Myriad (2013): isolated natural DNA not patentable as-is')
print('claim: synthetic constructs, modified sequences, methods of use')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.

title: GUI and Icon Design Patent
description: Graphical user interfaces and computer icons are protectable as design patents, with the drawings showing the icon or interface and broken lines disclaiming the underlying device. After Samsung v. Apple (2016), damages for design-patent infringement can be apportioned to the relevant article of manufacture rather than the whole product. Tech companies file these routinely alongside utility applications on the same product.
demo:
print('drawings: solid lines claim the GUI/icon; broken lines disclaim the device')
print('file alongside utility apps covering the same product')
provenance: Public reference: USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) and uspto.gov; verified 2026-10-21.
